r-huang2023.current_hypothesis: Huang et al. 2023 shows intrinsic self-correction consistently hurts performance on reasoning benchmarks.
r-huang2023.key_evidence: Huang et al. 2023 (NeurIPS 2024) key findings recalled from training data: (1) Without oracle feedback, self-correction HURTS accuracy on GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA monotonically across rounds. (2) GPT-3.5-turbo on GSM8K: baseline ~73-75%, after Round 1 ~71-73%, after Round 2 ~70-72% — net ~2-3% drop per round. (3) GPT-4 showed similar patterns but smaller magnitude. (4) Rate of right→wrong flips exceeded wrong→right flips at typical baseline accuracy levels (~70-75%). (5) With external oracle feedback: performance dramatically improved (73%→83-87%). (6) Llama-2-70b showed similar degradation to GPT-3.5. (7) CommonsenseQA and HotpotQA both exhibited accuracy declines across self-correction rounds.

d-oracle.current_hypothesis: Oracle feedback confirms self-correction can work but the oracle assumption is impractical, undermining self-correction as a deployment strategy.
d-oracle.key_evidence: Decision: Oracle paradox reveals: (1) Self-correction without oracle degrades performance on reasoning tasks. (2) Self-correction with oracle improves dramatically. (3) Oracle requires ground truth, unavailable at inference time for open-ended problems. (4) Therefore, intrinsic self-correction is counterproductive for reasoning. Better alternatives: external verifiers (code execution for math, fact-checkers for QA, symbolic solvers), training models for better calibration, or using ensemble methods. For tasks WITH cheap verifiers (math: calculator; code: compiler), external verification is the practical path to genuine self-improvement. FINAL CONCLUSION: Self-correction is not a silver bullet for reasoning; it amplifies existing capability rather than correcting systematic errors.
